# PRIOR ART — corv32

Researcher output for Step 1. Date of survey: 2026-10-04.

Method and caveats (read first):

- Every source below was opened on 2026-10-04 with WebFetch (or WebSearch followed by a fetch). The URL actually opened is recorded next to each item. Items I could not open are listed in section 7 and are NOT in `paper/refs.bib`.
- WebFetch passes pages through a small summarising model. Numbers marked **[raw]** were checked against raw README text or a PDF I read directly. Numbers marked **[summ]** come from a summarised page and should be re-read against the source before they go into the paper. Two PDFs (RISC-V specs, Gallmann CARRV, NoX) I rendered and read myself.
- All numbers here are PUBLISHED reference values, quoted as the source states them. They are not our measurements. The paper's comparisons must be measured by us on the same FPGA, same tools, same seeds (CLAUDE.md rule).
- The two single-author GitHub repositories in section 3.3 are unreviewed gray literature. I cite them only to show what already exists, not as evidence of correctness.

## 1. Headline findings for the Architect

1. **RISCOF is deprecated upstream.** The RISCOF repo says it is deprecated and points to ACT 4.0; the riscv-arch-test README says the ACT4 framework "replaces the deprecated riscof tool", uses the Sail reference model, and generates self-checking ELFs that run on the DUT's own testbench. The RISCOF Read the Docs page I opened (stable, v1.24.0) carries no deprecation notice. Decision needed (DECISIONS.md): (a) keep RISCOF with the legacy arch-test 3.x suite, (b) move to ACT4, or (c) do both. The task text and PLAN.md say RISCOF; the paper should say "RISC-V architectural tests (RISCOF/arch-test 3.x or ACT4, version stated)".
2. **The headline combination already exists in unreviewed form.** Two public hobby repos claim a 5-stage RV32IM(C) core with riscv-formal plus ISS lockstep plus CoreMark (section 3.3). They are not peer reviewed and neither compares against PicoRV32/VexRiscv on one FPGA, but they pre-empt "first to combine".
3. **>= 2 CoreMark/MHz is a weak bar.** Published numbers: Ibex "small" 2.47, VexRiscv full 2.30, DarkRISCV RV32IM 2.28, NoX 2.50 (RV32I), CV32E40P about 3. Gallmann et al. show a plain 2-stage Ibex goes from 1.58 to 2.36 CoreMark/MHz purely by compiler flags. Whatever number we report must carry the exact flags and the run length.
4. **CoreMark run rule and simulation.** The EEMBC rule is "at least 10 seconds". Ibex's published simulator flow hard-codes 10 iterations (its example: 4,244,465 cycles at 100 MHz, about 42 ms). If our headline number comes from Verilator, state iterations, clock assumption and that the 10 s rule is met in simulated time (or run on hardware: HARDWARE_TODO).
5. **riscv-formal is not a complete proof of ISA conformance.** Funck et al. (FDL 2023) mutate a riscv-formal-verified core (MicroRV32) and report that the evaluation "revealed several holes in riscv-formal". This supports a complementarity argument (formal plus lockstep plus arch tests), and gives us a method to measure it.

Bugs listed with the method that found each: divider operand race (random co-sim), minstret commit-point (riscv-tests), RVFI interrupt-flag corner case (formal), CSR latch (synthesis lint), branch-predictor flaw costing 11% IPC (profiling). [raw] | https://github.com/rkottomt/rv32imc-pipelined-core ; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rkottomt/rv32imc-pipelined-core/main/README.md |

Observations: the second repo is close to our whole plan on ECP5 (formal + lockstep + random + coverage + mutation + CoreMark + ECP5 Fmax) but uses a Python reference, not Spike, has no RISCOF, no PicoRV32/VexRiscv comparison, 34.7 MHz on ECP5, and no peer review. Both READMEs are the authors' own claims; I did not run anything. Its "bug found by method" list is exactly the kind of table our paper could produce with proper rigor.

ASIC (TSMC 65 nm), not FPGA. Numbers in section 3.1. | https://carrv.github.io/2021/papers/CARRV2021_paper_8_Gallmann.pdf |

## 5. Does prior work settle the claim?

The claim under test (from the task): a from-scratch five-stage RV32IM core that passes riscv-formal, passes the RISC-V architectural tests, matches Spike instruction-for-instruction on 1M random instructions, reaches at least 2 CoreMark/MHz, and is compared on Fmax/LUTs against PicoRV32 and VexRiscv on one FPGA with Yosys/nextpnr.

**Each ingredient exists and is routine.**
- riscv-formal: designed for exactly this; wrappers exist for PicoRV32, VexRiscv, SERV, NERV (in-tree), and Hazard3 carries a riscv-formal harness. Passing it is a known procedure (Wolf 2017; WARP-V; the two hobby repos).
- Architectural tests: NEORV32 and SERV publish passing compliance/ACT results. Not a differentiator, and the framework itself is mid-transition (RISCOF to ACT4).
- Lockstep against Spike: Ibex does this at scale with riscv-dv in a UVM environment, using RVFI. Dromajo and XiangShan-style difftest do it for larger cores. Doing it with Verilator plus Spike is a replication.
- >= 2 CoreMark/MHz in a small RV32IM core: Ibex small 2.47, VexRiscv 2.30 to 2.57, DarkRISCV 2.28, CV32E40P about 3, Hazard3 4.15. A 5-stage RV32IM with forwarding and a single-cycle multiplier is expected to clear 2.0; the bar is low and compiler-flag-dependent (Gallmann: 1.58 to 2.36 for the same 2-stage Ibex).
- The full combination in one small 5-stage RV32IM core: two unreviewed public repos already claim it (section 3.3), one on ECP5 with a 5-stage RV32IMC and 2.88 CoreMark/MHz. Hazard3 (3-stage) has riscv-formal and 4.15 CoreMark/MHz. Ibex has cosim and CoreMark but its docs say it is not yet formally verified.

**Therefore this project is an engineering replication of known practice, not a new method and not a first-of-its-kind artifact.** I would not let the paper claim novelty for "a core that passes all of formal, arch tests, lockstep and 2 CoreMark/MHz". At best it is a clean, fully reproducible, open instance of it, which is a legitimate artifact paper but a weak research contribution.

**What looks genuinely open (I searched but my search is not exhaustive; absence is a statement about what I found, not proof):**
1. **A same-toolchain, same-FPGA, multi-seed comparison.** Published PicoRV32/VexRiscv numbers are on Xilinx 7-series (README) or Cyclone, with vendor tools and unstated seeds. I found no published ECP5/nextpnr measurement for either core I could open (the Yosys+nextpnr paper has none). Modest but real, and fully ours to measure. Report median and spread over N nextpnr seeds, not a single run.
2. **Verification yield by method.** The literature evaluates riscv-formal (Funck 2023) and riscv-dv (Ahmadi-Pour 2021) separately, each with mutation, on different cores. The hobby repo above lists bugs per method but with 16 self-chosen mutants. I found no head-to-head study that injects one common, documented bug set into one core and reports which of {riscv-formal, arch tests, Spike lockstep with random programs, directed tests} kills each, with time-to-detection and instructions or CPU-seconds spent.
3. **Cost of reaching 2 CoreMark/MHz on an FPGA.** Gallmann et al. do the ablation (SBP, single-cycle mult, BT-ALU, WB stage) in ASIC kGE for Ibex. A per-feature ablation of a 5-stage core on ECP5 (LUT4, Fmax, CoreMark/MHz) with CoreMark flags fixed would be new data in that setting.

**Suggested sharper, falsifiable claims (pick one primary, keep the others as secondary results):**
- C-A (verification): "On a common set of N injected and naturally occurring RTL bugs in a 5-stage RV32IM core, riscv-formal finds the class X (forwarding, hazard, trap/CSR corner cases) bugs that 1M-instruction random lockstep against Spike misses, and lockstep finds class Y (long-latency interactions, divider/memory timing) bugs that bounded formal misses; arch tests alone detect fewer than Z%." Falsifiable by the kill matrix. Needs a pre-registered bug list (mutation operators fixed before running) and per-method effort metrics.
- C-B (cost): "On ECP5 with Yosys/nextpnr, reaching >= 2.0 CoreMark/MHz (stated flags, >= 10 s run) costs at most P LUT4 and Q% Fmax relative to the smallest configuration that passes all checks; no single feature (forwarding, 1-cycle multiplier, branch prediction) accounts for more than R of it." Falsifiable by ablation.
- C-C (benchmark): "Under identical Yosys/nextpnr settings and N seeds, corv32 exceeds PicoRV32 in CoreMark/MHz by a factor of at least F while using at most G times its LUT4s and keeping at least H% of its Fmax." Falsifiable but low novelty; use as the baseline-comparison section, not the thesis.

Recommendation: make C-A the thesis (with C-B and C-C as supporting evaluation). Be explicit in the paper that the verification toolset is standard and that the 2.0 CoreMark/MHz target is easily reachable. Do not claim 1M instructions of lockstep as strong coverage without reporting functional coverage (the hobby repo reports 234 bins; Funck shows formal also has holes).

## 6. Practical notes that affect the plan

- State RISCOF vs ACT4 choice, exact suite version, and the Sail/Spike reference used; ACT4 needs Sail, RISCOF 3.x-era flow used Spike or Sail as reference through plugins.
- RVFI wiring: the five-stage core must emit RVFI from the writeback stage; the lowRISC step-and-compare scheme (retired PC plus register write, then compare memory accesses, traps and interrupts) is a documented, reusable design for our Spike lockstep.
- CoreMark report line must include compiler version and flags (README rule). Gallmann shows flags move the score by up to about 1.5x on the same RTL; fix flags before measuring and publish them.
- Do not reuse any numbers from section 3 in the paper's own results tables; use them only in a clearly labelled "published reference values" table with platform column.

## 7. Not verified (excluded from refs.bib)

- Elsadek and Tawfik, "RISC-V Resource-Constrained Cores: A Survey and Energy Comparison", NEWCAS 2021 (DOI string seen only in a search result): paper itself not opened. Appears only through NoX Table III.
- Bordonaro, Rapuano, Bocchio, Fanucci, "Integration of the Open-Source RISC-V Formal Verification Framework into the STMicroelectronics Toolchain and Its Application to the STRiVe2.4 CPU" (Springer chapter, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-84100-2_6 per URL): Springer redirected to a login page; content not read. Claimed (via search snippet) to apply riscv-formal with JasperGold to an ST CPU.
- "Survey of Verification of RISC-V Processors" (Springer, J. Electron. Test. 2025, URL https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10836-025-06169-3): login redirect, not read. Worth a manual look; it may be the best peer-reviewed related-work survey.
- "Formal Verification of RISC-V Processor Chisel Designs" (Springer chapter, URL https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-96-0602-3_8) and Gao et al. FMCAD 2021 (CHERI-RISC-V end-to-end formal): seen only as search/listing results.
- "Effective Processor Verification with Logic Fuzzer Enhanced Co-simulation" (ResearchGate, 403): not read.
- Hennessy and Patterson ACM DL pages (403) and the 2018 RISC-V Workshop slides by Humbenberger and Wolf (404): not opened. Only the Elsevier listing pages were read for the textbooks.
- A PicoRV32 ECP5 figure ("9,957 LUT4, Fmax 30.64 MHz") appeared in a search summary with no opened primary source. Dropped. The kernellum issue and nextpnr `ice40/picorv32_benchmark.py` I opened contain no such numbers (the latter targets iCE40 HX8K and prints min/avg/max over 8 seeds, a useful methodology precedent for our seed sweep: https://github.com/YosysHQ/nextpnr/blob/main/ice40/picorv32_benchmark.py).
- Lattice/Xilinx vendor datasheets, LiteX VexRiscv-on-ECP5 numbers: not found in an openable primary source.
- GitHub star counts, last-commit dates and license types for the two hobby repos were not reliably extracted.

## 8. Source count

53 entries in `paper/refs.bib`, all opened. Of the web fetches, the following were PDFs read directly (page images): RISC-V Unprivileged and Privileged manuals (title and TOC pages), Funck FDL 2023 (pp. 1-2), Ahmadi-Pour MBMV 2021 (pp. 1-2), Gallmann CARRV 2021 (pp. 1-5), NoX (reference page and Tables I-III), Yosys+nextpnr (pp. 3-5). The rest are README/HTML pages passed through the fetch summariser, tagged [raw] where I requested verbatim quotes of the raw file and [summ] otherwise.
